faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 (weeks per year). For a standard full-time role of 38 hours per week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52 = annual gross salary. This assumes no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and an award rate for IT roles?

Many IT professionals are covered by awards such as the Professional Employees Award or the Clerks Award, which set higher minimum rates based on classification and experience. Always check the applicable award via the Fair Work Ombudsman pay guides.

faqs.q: How is casual loading applied, and does super get paid on top?
faqs.a: Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the minimum hourly rate (e.g., $33.05 per hour for the National Minimum Wage). Superannuation is calculated at 12% of ordinary earnings and is paid on top of the gross salary, not deducted from it. The super guarantee is capped at the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year.

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Your IT Salary: Hourly to Annual

Whether you are negotiating a new role or checking your current pay, understanding how an hourly rate translates to an annual salary is essential. The standard conversion used across Australia is based on a 38-hour full-time week, as set by the Fair Work Commission. This guide explains the formula, distinguishes between the National Minimum Wage and award rates, and covers casual loading, superannuation, and tax.

### The Basic Formula

Annual gross salary = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks.

For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, the calculation is:

**Hourly rate × 38 × 52 = annual gross salary**

For example, at the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour, the annual gross is $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,260 (rounded). If you are paid fortnightly, your gross pay would be approximately $2,010 per fortnight (weekly pay × 2). This estimate assumes the same rate every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 ordinary hours. This rate applies to award/agreement-free employees aged 21 and over. However, many IT professionals are covered by an award, such as the Professional Employees Award or the Clerks Award, which often set higher minimum rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides pay guides for each award, listing classification-specific rates. Always check which award applies to your role to ensure you are paid correctly.

### Casual Loading and Superannuation

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. For the National Minimum Wage, that means $33.05 per hour. This loading compensates for the lack of paid leave. When using our [timesheet](/), you can tick the casual loading checkbox to add 25% to your base rate – never enter a rate that already includes loading.

Superannuation is paid on top of your gross salary. The super guarantee is 12% of ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For example, on a $52,260 annual salary, the employer would contribute an additional $6,271.20 in super. This is not deducted from your pay; it is an extra benefit.

### Estimating Tax and Take-Home Pay

For the 2026–27 financial year, resident tax rates are:
- Nil up to $18,200
- 15% from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% above $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (using the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds). Using our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) estimator, you can see what your net pay might be after tax and Medicare. Remember, this is an estimate only – it does not include HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging.

### Why the 38-Hour Week Matters for Your IT Salary

When discussing your **it salary**, always clarify the weekly hours. Many IT roles are advertised as 38 hours per week, but some may be 37.5 or 40. Using the standard 38-hour assumption ensures consistency with the National Minimum Wage and most awards. If your role is part-time or casual, adjust the hours accordingly. For a quick reference, see our [reference tables](/data) for common hourly-to-annual conversions.

### Fortnightly Pay and Budgeting

If you are paid fortnightly, multiply your weekly gross by two. For a full-time employee on the National Minimum Wage, that is approximately $2,010 per fortnight before tax. This can help with budgeting and comparing job offers. Our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool lets you switch between hourly, weekly, fortnightly, and annual figures.

### Award-Free vs Award-Covered Employees

If you are not covered by an award or enterprise agreement, the National Minimum Wage is your floor. However, many IT contractors and employees fall under awards that specify higher rates for classifications such as Level 1, Level 2, or Senior Professional. The Fair Work Ombudsman’s pay guides are the authoritative source for these rates. For award-free employees, the special national minimum wages apply for juniors, apprentices, and those with disabilities.

### Using the Timesheet Tool

Our [timesheet](/) allows you to enter your base hourly rate and optionally add casual loading. The tool then calculates your annual gross, fortnightly pay, estimated tax, and super. It assumes a 38-hour week unless you adjust the hours. Remember that super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

### Final Thoughts

Whether you are comparing a job offer or checking your current pay, understanding the conversion from hourly to annual is key. Use the National Minimum Wage as a baseline, but always check the relevant award for your IT role. For more details on award rates, visit the [pay guides](/blog) page. And for a deeper dive into superannuation and salary packaging, see our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) guide.
